claim: The age distribution of incident cases provides a more robust picture of trends in transmission than overall incidence for most immunizing infections.
source: For most immunizing infections, the age distribution of incident cases provides a more robust picture of trends in transmission.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle about immunizing infections and surveillance.

claim: The framework estimates transmission intensity for dengue virus from age-specific incidence data for 359 administrative units in Thailand, Colombia, Brazil and Mexico.
source: We present a framework to estimate transmission intensity for dengue virus from age-specific incidence data, and apply it to 359 administrative units in Thailand, Colombia, Brazil and Mexico.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of administrative units analyzed.

claim: The estimates correlate well with those derived from seroprevalence data.
source: Our estimates correlate well with those derived from seroprevalence data (the gold standard)
evidence: The abstract states this correlation, which is supported by data presented in the results.

claim: The estimates capture the expected spatial heterogeneity in risk.
source: Our estimates correlate well with those derived from seroprevalence data (the gold standard), capture the expected spatial heterogeneity in risk
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by results showing variation across administrative units.

claim: The estimates correlate with known environmental drivers of transmission.
source: Our estimates correlate well with those derived from seroprevalence data (the gold standard), capture the expected spatial heterogeneity in risk, and correlate with known environmental drivers of transmission.
evidence: The abstract states this correlation, which is validated in the results section with specific environmental variables.

claim: Age-specific counts are routinely collected by many surveillance systems.
source: Since age-specific counts are routinely collected by masany surveillance systems, they represent a unique opportunity to further our understanding of disease burden and risk for many diseases.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about surveillance practices.

claim: The quality of surveillance often differs significantly both across countries and within regions of a country.
source: However, the use of raw case counts, or incidences, as a measure of disease risk can frequently be misleading because the quality of surveillance often differs significantly both across countries and within regions of a country making comparisons inappropriate.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of surveillance systems.

claim: Areas with more complete reporting of disease may inaccurately appear to have more disease simply because reported cases scale linearly with completeness of reporting.
source: Areas with more complete reporting of disease may inaccurately appear to have more disease simply because reported cases scale linearly with completeness of reporting.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of differences in reporting completeness.

claim: Serological surveys are regarded as the gold standard to measure the susceptible fraction and infer the extent of transmission for most immunizing infections.
source: For most immunizing infections (infections that generate long-lasting sterilizing immunity), serological surveys are regarded as the gold standard to measure the susceptible fraction and infer the extent of transmission
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus.

claim: An extensive review of the dengue literature found only three population-based serosurveys conducted in Brazil over the past 10 years.
source: For example, an extensive review of the dengue literature published recently found only three population-based serosurveys conducted in Brazil over the past 10 years, despite being the country that currently reports the largest number of cases worldwide (Fritzell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fritzell et al., 2018.

claim: Only one serosurvey was identified for the Philippines and three for Thailand despite high dengue burden.
source: Similarly, only one and three studies were identified for the Philippines and Thailand, respectively, even though the burden of dengue is very high (Fritzell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fritzell et al., 2018.

claim: The age distribution of cases is largely robust to under-reporting.
source: Importantly, the age distributionof cases is also largely robust to under-reporting, facilitating the comparison between locations or over time.
evidence: This is stated as a key property of age-specific data.

claim: Dengue is the most widely spread mosquito-transmitted virus.
source: Dengue is a relevant example because, despite being the most widely spread mosquito-transmitted virus, large gaps remain in our understanding of its global and local epidemiology (Fritzell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Large gaps remain in our understanding of dengue's global and local epidemiology.
source: Dengue is a relevant example because, despite being the most widely spread mosquito-transmitted virus, large gaps remain in our understanding of its global and local epidemiology (Fritzell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The average force of infection over the last 20 years was estimated for 148 administrative level one units.
source: We estimated the average forces of infection (FOI) over the last 20 years for 148 administrative level one units where age specific case data was available (Table 1, Figure 1B): 72/76 provinces of Thailand, 28/32 departments of Colombia, 21/27 states of Brazil, and 27/31 states of Mexico.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis performed.

claim: The administrative units analyzed comprise 90%, 99%, 90% and 91% of the population at risk in Thailand, Colombia, Brazil and Mexico respectively.
source: These administrative units comprise 90%, 99%, 90% and 91% of the population at risk of these countries respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the coverage of the analysis.

claim: Forces of infection were estimated for 211 municipalities (administrative level two units) of Colombia where at least 200 cases were reported.
source: We also estimated forces of infection for 211 municipalities (administrative level two units) of Colombia where at least 200 cases were reported over the period covered by the data.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis performed.

claim: The average FOI was 0.096 (95%CI 0.092-0.100) in Thailand.
source: The average FOI (the rate at which susceptible individuals that will become infected in a year by any dengue serotype) was 0.096 in Thailand (95%CI 0.092-0.100)
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: The average FOI was 0.132 (95%CI 0.128-0.136) in Colombia.
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: The average FOI was 0.124 (95%CI 0.116-0.128) in Brazil.
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: The average FOI was 0.052 (95%CI 0.048-0.056) in Mexico.
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: 12% of the susceptible population of Colombia and Brazil get infected yearly.
source: Similarly, 12% of the susceptible population of Colombia and Brazil, and 5% of the susceptible population of Mexico get infected yearly.
evidence: This is calculated from the FOI estimates.

claim: 5% of the susceptible population of Mexico get infected yearly.
source: Similarly, 12% of the susceptible population of Colombia and Brazil, and 5% of the susceptible population of Mexico get infected yearly.
evidence: This is calculated from the FOI estimates.

claim: Transmission intensity varied greatly within countries.
source: However, as expected, transmission intensity varied greatly within countries
evidence: This is stated as a finding with supporting data on ranges and coefficients of variation.

claim: FOI ranged between 0.04 and 0.15 (coefficient of variation = 0.27) across provinces of Thailand.
source: ranging between 0.04 and 0.15 (coefficient of variation (CV) = 0.27) across provinces of Thailand
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: FOI ranged between 0.02 and 0.20 (CV = 0.37) across departments of Colombia.
source: between 0.02 and 0.20 across departments of Colombia (CV = 0.37)
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: FOI ranged between 0.02 and 0.24 (CV = 0.56) across states of Brazil.
source: between 0.02 and 0.24 across states of Brazil (CV = 0.56)
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: FOI ranged between 0.01 and 0.092 (CV = 0.45) across states of Mexico.
source: between 0.01 and 0.092 across states of Mexico (CV = 0.45)
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: Transmission was highest in the North East of Brazil with an average FOI of 0.152.
source: Transmission was highest in the North East of Brazil (average FOI of 0.152)
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: Transmission was highest in the Caribbean region of Colombia with an average FOI of 0.156.
source: and in the Caribbean region of Colombia (average FOI of 0.156)
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: There was substantial heterogeneity within departments of Colombia.
source: There was also substantial heterogeneity within departments of Colombia.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with supporting data on coefficient of variation.

claim: The mean coefficient of variation for 15 departments of Colombia where estimates were available for more than 5 municipalities was 0.4.
source: The mean CV for 15 departments where we had estimates for more than 5 municipalities was 0.4.
evidence: This is a direct result from the statistical analysis.

claim: Good correlation (R2 = 0.73, 95% CI 0.51–0.87) was found between FOI estimates derived from case data and those from serological data for 16 locations.
source: For the 16 locations where we had access to both age-stratified serological data (the gold standard) and case data, we found good correlation between the estimates of the FOI derived from both data sources (R2 = 0.73, 95% CI 0.51–0.87, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the validation analysis comparing two data sources.

claim: No correlation (R2 = 0.002) was found between recent incidence of dengue and FOI estimates derived from serological data.
source: In contrast, we found no correlation between recent incidence of dengue in these locations (the average yearly incidence over the most recent 5 years of data) and the estimates of FOI derived from serological data (R2 = 0.002, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the validation analysis.

claim: FOI increased by 0.006 (95% CI 0.004–0.007, R2 = 0.19) for each additional °C in temperature for 211 Colombian municipalities.
source: On average, the FOI increased by 0.006 (95% CI 0.004–0.007, R2 = 0.19) for each additional °C in temperature
evidence: This is a direct result from the regression analysis of environmental drivers.

claim: FOI decreased by 0.005 (95% CI 0.003, 0.006, R2 = 0.21) for each 100 m increase in elevation for 211 Colombian municipalities.
source: it decreased by 0.005 (95% CI 0.003, 0.006, R2 = 0.21) for each 100 m increase in elevation (Table 2)
evidence: This is a direct result from the regression analysis of environmental drivers.

claim: Population density was not associated with FOI estimates in unadjusted analyses.
source: While population density was not associated with FOI estimates in unadjusted analyses
evidence: This is a direct result from the regression analysis.

claim: A twofold increase in population density was associated with a 0.007 (95% 0.004–0.009) increase in FOI in the best fitting adjusted model.
source: a twofold increase in density was associated with a 0.007 (95% 0.004–0.009) increase in FOI in the best fitting adjusted model
evidence: This is a direct result from the adjusted regression analysis.

claim: The best fitting adjusted model included elevation, population density and precipitation, and explained 35% (95%CI 23–50%) of the variance.
source: This model included elevation, population density and precipitation, and explained 35% (95%CI 23–50%) of the variance.
evidence: This is a direct result from the regression analysis.

claim: Recent incidence of dengue in Colombian municipalities was not correlated with temperature (R2 = 0.01).
source: In contrast, the recent incidence of dengue in these municipalities was not correlated with temperature, elevation or Aedes aegypti abundance (R2 0.01, 0.01, and 0.00 respectively, Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from the regression analysis comparing incidence with environmental drivers.

claim: Recent incidence of dengue in Colombian municipalities was not correlated with elevation (R2 = 0.01).
source: In contrast, the recent incidence of dengue in these municipalities was not correlated with temperature, elevation or Aedes aegypti abundance (R2 0.01, 0.01, and 0.00 respectively, Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from the regression analysis comparing incidence with environmental drivers.

claim: Recent incidence of dengue in Colombian municipalities was not correlated with Aedes aegypti abundance (R2 = 0.00).
source: In contrast, the recent incidence of dengue in these municipalities was not correlated with temperature, elevation or Aedes aegypti abundance (R2 0.01, 0.01, and 0.00 respectively, Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct result from the regression analysis comparing incidence with environmental drivers.

claim: A negative association was found between population density and incidence, indicating a 6% (95%CI 2–10%) decrease in log incidence for each 2-fold increase in population density.
source: We did find a negative association between population density and incidence, indicating a 6% (95%CI 2–10%) decrease in log incidence for each 2-fold increase in population density.
evidence: This is a direct result from the regression analysis.

claim: The only available dengue vaccine (Dengvaxia) has been licensed for use in children 9 years or older in 20 countries including Thailand, Brazil and Mexico.
source: The only available dengue vaccine (Dengvaxia) has been licensed for use in children 9 years or older in 20 countries including Thailand, Brazil and Mexico.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about vaccine licensing.

claim: The WHO currently recommends confirmation of prior dengue infection at the individual level before vaccinating individuals.
source: The WHO currently recommends confirmation (by virology or serology) of prior dengue infection at the individual level before vaccinating individuals, and therefore there is interest in identifying populations with high seropositivity to target pre-vaccination screening (WHO, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to WHO 2018 guidelines.

claim: An alternative vaccination strategy discussed is rolling out the vaccine in settings with 80% or greater seropositivity among 9 year olds.
source: In the absence of appropriate rapid serological assays that would allow implementing this individual screening strategy, an alternative that has been discussed is rolling out the vaccine in settings with 80% or greater seropositivity among 9 year olds.
evidence: This is stated as a discussed alternative strategy.

claim: Only a small minority of locations in Colombia and Brazil have > 80% seropositivity in 9 year olds.
source: Our results suggest that only a small minority of locations in Colombia and Brazil have > 80% seropositivity in this age group (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: The expected proportion seropositive at 9 years of age ranged between 0.35 and 0.75 in provinces of Thailand.
source: The expected proportion seropositive at 9 years of age ranged between 0.35 and 0.75 in provinces of Thailand
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: The expected proportion seropositive at 9 years of age ranged between 0.13 and 0.85 in departments of Colombia.
source: 0.13 and 0.85 in departments of Colombia
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: The expected proportion seropositive at 9 years of age ranged between 0 and 0.88 in states of Brazil.
source: 0 and 0.88 in states of Brazil
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: The expected proportion seropositive at 9 years of age ranged between 0.07 and 0.56 in states of Mexico.
source: 0.07 and 0.56 in states of Mexico
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: Seroprevalence was estimated to be high enough (≥80%) in only 2/28 Colombian departments.
source: The seroprevalence was estimated to be high enough in only 2/28 Colombian departments
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: Seroprevalence was estimated to be high enough (≥80%) in only 4/25 Brazilian states.
source: 4/25 Brazilian states
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: None of the 72 Thai provinces reached 80% seroprevalence at age 9.
source: none of the 72 Thai provinces or 27 Mexican states
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: None of the 27 Mexican states reached 80% seroprevalence at age 9.
source: none of the 72 Thai provinces or 27 Mexican states
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence.

claim: Within the two Colombian departments that met the 80% seroprevalence threshold, only 9/13 (70%) of the municipalities evaluated reached this level.
source: Furthermore, even within the two Colombian departments that met the 80% seroprevalence threshold, only 9/13 (70%) of the municipalities evaluated reached this level.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of expected seroprevalence at municipality level.

claim: It would be necessary to target children 14 years of age or older in over 70% (108/148) of locations to comply with WHO-SAGE recommendations.
source: Our results suggest that, to comply with the WHO-SAGE recommendations, it would be necessary to target children 14 years of age or older in over 70% (108/148) of locations.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of minimum age for vaccination.

claim: In approximately 50% of the locations evaluated, it would be necessary to target individuals aged 18 years or older, precluding school-based vaccination strategies.
source: Furthermore, in approximately 50% of the locations evaluated, it would be necessary to target individuals aged 18 years or older, precluding school-based vaccination strategies.
evidence: This is a direct result from the analysis of minimum age for vaccination.

claim: Both the incidence and the mean adjusted incidence performed very poorly in ranking spatial units compared to the FOI.
source: Both the incidence and the mean adjusted incidence performed very poorly in ranking spatial units compared to the FOI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the comparison of alternative metrics.

claim: The proportion of incidence under 10 years and the mean age of cases performed quite well at ranking spatial units within countries.
source: In contrast, the proportion of incidence under 10 years and the mean age of cases (to a lesser degree) performed quite well at ranking spatial units within countries.
evidence: This is a direct result from the comparison of alternative metrics.

claim: None of the alternative metrics performed as well as the FOI when comparing spatial units from different countries.
source: However, none of these metrics performed as well as the FOI when comparing spatial units from different countries, and they did not correlate as well with the gold standard (FOI estimates derived from seroprevalence data) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the comparison of alternative metrics.

claim: Estimates derived from all cases tended to underestimate those obtained from DHF cases.
source: In general, estimates derived from all cases tended to underestimate those obtained from DHF cases, but the correlation between the estimates was good (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is a direct result from the sensitivity analysis comparing different case definitions.

claim: The correlation between FOI estimates from all cases vs. DHF cases was highest for Colombia (r = 0.74) and Mexico (r = 0.78).
source: The correlation was highest for Colombia and Mexico (r = 0.74 and r = 0.78, respectively)
evidence: This is a direct result from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The correlation between FOI estimates from all cases vs. DHF cases was lower for Brazil (r = 0.48).
source: but less so for Brazil (r = 0.48)
evidence: This is a direct result from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: 2/3 of the Brazilian locations that showed discrepant results had the smallest number of DHF cases (n = 217 and 265).
source: However, 2/3 of the Brazilian locations that showed discrepant results had the smallest number of DHF cases (n = 217 and 265) suggesting that sample size may have played a role.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the sensitivity analysis with inference about sample size effects.

claim: All the Colombian locations where there was a large discrepancy had very low counts of DHF cases (n = 41, 55, and 48, respectively).
source: Similarly, all the Colombian locations where there was a large discrepancy had very low counts of DHF cases (n = 41, 55, and 48, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: For immunizing infections in endemic circulation, recent incidence may be a poor metric of transmission and may be misleading when ranking spatial units.
source: Our results underscore the extent to which, for immunizing infections in endemic circulation, recent incidence may be a poor metric of transmission and may be misleading when ranking spatial units (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results with supporting figure.

claim: Immunity of the population in high-transmission settings reduces the number of individuals that are susceptible to infection.
source: Immunity of the population in high-transmission settings reduces the number of individuals that are susceptible to infection.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why incidence may be misleading.

claim: Incidence in places where transmission intensity is lower may be roughly equivalent to that in higher transmission intensity areas.
source: As a result, incidence in places where transmission intensity is lower, but people remain susceptible for a longer period of time, may be roughly equivalent to that in higher transmission intensity areas.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why incidence may be misleading.

claim: FOI estimates are more robust to differences in surveillance efficiency than aggregate counts.
source: Since FOI estimates are derived from the age distribution of incidence, and not from the aggregate counts, they are more robust to differences in surveillance efficiency and can be obtained with relatively small numbers of yearly cases.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of the FOI approach.

claim: FOI estimates can be obtained with relatively small numbers of yearly cases.
source: Since FOI estimates are derived from the age distribution of incidence, and not from the aggregate counts, they are more robust to differences in surveillance efficiency and can be obtained with relatively small numbers of yearly cases.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of the FOI approach.

claim: As much as 35% of the variance in FOI may be explained by differences in temperature/elevation and population density alone.
source: While this heterogeneity is probably driven by multiple environmental, socio-economic and demographic factors, our results suggest that as much as 35% of the variance may be explained by differences in temperature/elevation and population density alone.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the regression analysis.

claim: Northeastern Brazil was the region that experienced the highest incidence of Zika during the 2015/2016 epidemic.
source: Northeastern Brazil was also the region that experienced the highest incidence of Zika during the 2015/2016 epidemic, and this is not surprising given that both viruses are transmitted by the same mosquito vector (A. aegypti)(Lowe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Both dengue and Zika viruses are transmitted by the same mosquito vector (A. aegypti).
source: Northeastern Brazil was also the region that experienced the highest incidence of Zika during the 2015/2016 epidemic, and this is not surprising given that both viruses are transmitted by the same mosquito vector (A. aegypti)(Lowe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The high transmission intensities found in Northeastern Brazil suggest that this region might be ideal to implement pre-vaccination screening strategies.
source: For example, the high transmission intensities (and expected seroprevalences) found in Northeastern Brazil suggest that this region might be ideal to implement pre-vaccination screening strategies.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the FOI estimates for vaccination policy.

claim: The large heterogeneity estimated in Colombia suggests that decisions of where to deploy control interventions should be made at least at the municipal/district (administrative level 2) level.
source: In addition, the large heterogeneity estimated in Colombia suggests that decisions of where to deploy control interventions, including vaccines, should be made at least at the municipal/district (administrative level 2) level.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the heterogeneity findings.

claim: The case-definition of DHF is quite specific.
source: While the case-definition of DHF is quite specific, milder forms of the disease are characterized by a non-specific febrile syndrome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dengue case definitions.

claim: Milder forms of dengue are characterized by a non-specific febrile syndrome.
source: While the case-definition of DHF is quite specific, milder forms of the disease are characterized by a non-specific febrile syndrome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dengue case definitions.

claim: Data from locations that report 'all cases' rather than more severe forms (DHF) are more likely to be misclassified.
source: Therefore, data from locations that report 'all cases' rather than more severe forms (DHF) are more likely to be misclassified, and could be less useful to infer transmission histories.
evidence: This is stated as a concern about data quality with logical inference.

claim: The model assumes that the age distribution of cases represents the age distribution of secondary infections.
source: It assumes that the age distribution of cases represents the age distribution of secondary infections, thus ignoring the potential contribution of primary, tertiary and quaternary infections.
evidence: This is stated as a model assumption.

claim: The model assumes that risk of infection, symptoms, and health seeking behavior are not age dependent.
source: It also assumes that risk of infection, symptoms, and health seeking behavior are not age dependent, even though there is some evidence that suggests that this may not be the case(Katzelnick et al., 2018; Guzmán and Kourí, 2002; Thai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a model assumption with citation to evidence that may contradict it.

claim: The model assumes equal circulation of all serotypes.
source: It assumes equal circulation of all serotypes, despite the known dominance of specific serotypes for extended periods of time in the Americas (Katzelnick et al., 2018; Teixeira et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a model assumption with citation to evidence that may contradict it.

claim: Specific serotypes have been known to dominate for extended periods of time in the Americas.
source: It assumes equal circulation of all serotypes, despite the known dominance of specific serotypes for extended periods of time in the Americas (Katzelnick et al., 2018; Teixeira et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The model estimates transmission intensities over extended periods of time (20 years), averaging over variations in the FOI that may occur at shorter time scales.
source: Finally, it estimates transmission intensities over extended periods of time (20 years), averaging over variations in the FOI that may occur at shorter time scales.
evidence: This is stated as a model limitation.

claim: Some discrepancy between FOI estimates from case data and those from seroprevalence data is expected as the two sources of data do not represent exactly the same period of time and location.
source: While further validation is desirable, it is important to note that some discrepancy between our estimates and those derived from seroprevalence data is expected as the two sources of data do not represent exactly the same period of time and location.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for observed discrepancies.

claim: Most of the serosurveys available were conducted in specific urban centers, while case data represents the full administrative unit.
source: For example, most of the serosurveys available were conducted in specific urban centers, while case data represents the full administrative unit.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for observed discrepancies.

claim: The same approach should be generalizable to other immunizing infections including chikungunya and Zika.
source: While here we focus on dengue, the same approach should be generalizable to other immunizing infections including chikungunya and Zika.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about the generalizability of the method.

claim: The WHO's SAGE committee recommended in April 2016 that dengue vaccine only be used in settings with known high endemicity, defined as places where seroprevalence is greater than 70% in the target vaccination age-group.
source: Due to uncertainty regarding the vaccine's benefits and risks in individuals who haven't been previously infected by dengue, the WHO's scientific advisory group of experts (SAGE) committee recommended in April 2016 that this vaccine only be used in settings with known high endemicity, defined as places where seroprevalence is greater than 70% in the target vaccination age-group (SAGE, 2016)
evidence: This is stated with citation to SAGE 2016.

claim: The WHO's SAGE committee recommended that dengue vaccine should not be used in places where seroprevalence is under 50%.
source: and should not be used in places where seroprevalence is under 50%.
evidence: This is stated as part of the SAGE recommendation.

claim: The WHO now recommends that individuals should be tested for dengue antibodies prior to vaccination.
source: This recommendation was later revised, and the WHO now recommends that individuals should be tested for dengue antibodies prior to vaccination, and the vaccine should only be given to individuals who have been infected by dengue in the past (WHO, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to WHO 2018.

claim: The vaccine should only be given to individuals who have been infected by dengue in the past.
source: This recommendation was later revised, and the WHO now recommends that individuals should be tested for dengue antibodies prior to vaccination, and the vaccine should only be given to individuals who have been infected by dengue in the past (WHO, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to WHO 2018.

claim: These estimates were made available online in June 2017 as a tool to help countries deciding where to target vaccination.
source: In collaboration with the MRC center for Outbreak Analysis and Modeling, these estimates were made available online in June 2017 (https://mrcdata.dide.ic.ac.uk/_dengue/dengue.php) as a tool to help countries deciding where to target vaccination.
evidence: This is stated as a description of how the results were disseminated.

claim: Data on yearly age-specific reported number of dengue cases was used for administrative level 1 units of Thailand, Colombia, Brazil and Mexico.
source: We used data on the yearly age-specific reported number of dengue cases for administrative level 1 units of Thailand, Colombia, Brazil and Mexico (Ministério da Saude, 2017; Bureau of Epidemiology, Department of Disease Control, 2019; Direccion General de Epidemiología, 2017; Instituto Nacional de Salud Colombia, 2016)
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data sources used.

claim: The period of time available for data varied between countries, ranging between 5 years in Colombia and 25 years in Thailand.
source: The period of time available varied between countries, but ranged between 5 years in Colombia and 25 years in Thailand.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data availability.

claim: Age-specific case reports on dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) were used for Thailand and Brazil where possible.
source: Where possible (Thailand and Brazil) we used age-specific case reports on dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) for our analyses.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data type used.

claim: For Colombia and Mexico, data on all reported dengue cases was used because the number of DHF cases reported by a substantial number of spatial units were insufficient to estimate the FOI.
source: However, for both Colombia and Mexico, we had to use data on all reported dengue cases because the number of DHF cases reported by a substantial number of spatial units (9/32 units in Colombia and 10/31 in mexico) were insufficient to estimate the FOI.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the data type used.

claim: The model was fit in a Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework using the RStan package in R.
source: We fit the model in a Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework using the RStan package in R (Stan development Team, 2019) (The R Foundation, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: Four independent chains were simulated, each of 30000 iterations, discarding the first 10000 iterations as warm-up.
source: We simulated four independent chains, each of 30000 iterations and discarded the firs 10000 iterations as warm-up.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the MCMC implementation.

claim: Convergence was assessed visually and using Rubin's R statistic.
source: We assessed convergence visually and using Rubin's R statistic.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model validation approach.

claim: 95% credible intervals were obtained from the 2.5% and 97.5% percentiles of the posterior distributions.
source: We obtained 95% credible intervals from the 2.5% and 97.5% percentiles of the posterior distributions.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the uncertainty quantification approach.

claim: The FOI has varied substantially over time in many of the settings considered.
source: Since it is known that the FOI has varied substantially over time in many of the settings considered, we allowed λ(t) to vary as a function of time.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge justifying the modeling approach.

claim: Constant λ(t) was assumed for periods of 20 years to limit the number of parameters estimated.
source: To limit the number of parameters estimated, we assumed constant λ(t) for periods of 20 years.
evidence: This is stated as a modeling decision.

claim: The majority of dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) cases arise from secondary infections according to data from Thailand.
source: Data from Thailand has consistently suggested that the majority of dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) cases arise from secondary infections (Burke et al., 1988)
evidence: This is stated with citation to Burke et al., 1988.

claim: Methods to estimate transmission parameters from age-stratified serological data have been available for many years.
source: Methods to estimate transmission parameters from age-stratified serological data have been available for many years(Muench, 1959)
evidence: This is stated with citation to Muench, 1959.

claim: Methods to estimate dengue forces of infection from case data have been applied to settings where dengue is thought to be close to endemic circulation.
source: Methods to estimate dengue forces of infection from case data have been applied to settings where dengue is thought to be close to endemic circulation (Cummings et al., 2009; Imai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: In settings with high endemic transmission, incident cases are expected to be concentrated in younger age groups, as adults are likely to be already immune.
source: In settings with high endemic transmission, incident cases are expected to be concentrated in younger age groups, as adults are likely to be already immune (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an expected pattern with supporting figure.

claim: In places where there is less population immunity, the age distribution of cases is more likely to resemble the age distribution of the population itself.
source: In contrast, in places where there is less population immunity, the age distribution of cases is more likely to resemble the age distribution of the population itself, with cases in in both children and adult populations.
evidence: This is stated as an expected pattern.
